title: Plan, write and improve a short text
intro: I can write for a familiar reader, organise my ideas and edit my words so the message is clear.
exampleTitle: A precise edit helps the reader
example: Original draft: “Mila put a thing in the garden. She was carrying it.” The reader cannot tell what the thing is or which action came first. Revised: “Mila was carrying a small seed tray. She put the tray in the garden.” Naming the tray and putting the carrying before the placing makes the events clear. The noun group “a small seed tray” names and describes the object; the whole verb group “was carrying” tells what Mila was doing.
steps: 1. Choose a purpose and organise ideas

Decide who will read your text and what you want it to do. A story links events; information groups facts; persuasion states a view and gives a relevant reason. Read the three complete original model texts below.

For classmates, the story follows a lost note and its return. The library information groups facts under headings. The class request asks for a reading box and explains its benefit. Each has a different job.
Plan a short story for a classmate: A paper hat blows away in the playground. Who helps, what happens next and how does it end?

Accept different coherent plans. For example: Jo loses the hat; Lee catches it beside the bench; Jo thanks Lee and puts it in a bag. The response solves the problem. Write the linked events so a reader can follow them, rather than listing unrelated ideas.
2. Make sentences and word groups work

A simple sentence can express one complete message. To make a compound sentence, join two messages that can each stand alone, using a link such as and, but or so. Choose words that make the connection clear.

“The box was full.” is simple. “The box was full, so Amir chose another box.” joins two complete messages and shows a result. In “The small seed tray was resting on the shelf”, “The small seed tray” is a noun group and “was resting” is the whole verb group.
Join “The path was muddy.” and “We wore boots.” to show a result. Then replace “thing” in “We filled the thing with soil” with a precise gardening word.

One answer is “The path was muddy, so we wore boots.” Both parts are complete messages; so shows the result. “We filled the seed tray with soil” uses a precise topic word. A pot or planter can also fit if that is the intended object. Keep the meaning accurate.
3. Reread, edit and make a multimodal version

Check meaning and order first. Add a missing detail, delete needless repetition or replace an unclear word. Then check sentence grammar, capitals, end marks and spelling. A pronoun such as she or it must point clearly to the intended person or thing.

Draft: “sam took the basket to the garden. He put it it by the gate” Revised: “Sam took the basket to the garden. He put it by the gate.” Sam needs a capital, one it is deleted and the final full stop is added. He refers to Sam; it refers to the basket. Basket and garden are common two-syllable words.
Edit “lena carried a thing to the garden. He put it by the shed” so Lena carries a seed tray. In this story Lena uses she. What should change?

Write “Lena carried a seed tray to the garden. She put it by the shed.” Name the intended object, use Lena’s capital and the supplied pronoun she, and finish both sentences. Then create a drawing and matching caption, or an adult-supported digital version, using the steps below.
mistakes: “Editing means fixing spelling only.”
Check whether the ideas make sense and are in a useful order as well as checking spelling and punctuation.
“Every and makes a compound sentence.”
“Mila packed seeds and soil” joins two things. It has one complete message. Check for two complete messages before calling a sentence compound.
“A longer word always improves writing.”
Choose a precise word that helps this reader. Seed tray is useful when that is what you mean.
activity: Choose one of the complete planning cards in More examples. Write a short story, information text or persuasive request for the named familiar reader. Read it back, make one meaning edit and one convention edit, and explain how each helps. Across later short sessions, try the other two purposes. Add a drawing with a useful caption if it helps your reader.
adjust: Starter: tell an adult your ideas, then write one sentence with a word bank. Core: write a short organised text with a simple sentence, a true compound sentence and a precise topic word. Stretch: change the purpose or reader and explain which structure and wording you revised.
safety: An adult can read directions and help use a familiar device. Keep the learner’s own choices visible and note dictated or modelled support. The digital task saves locally with adult help; it needs no account, upload or personal information.
tricky: 1. Is “Lena packed seeds and pots” a compound sentence?
Under this lesson’s primary-school convention, no. And links two objects, not two complete messages. “Lena packed seeds, and Kai carried the pots” has two complete messages.
2. Must I use the longest possible noun group?
No. Include the words that identify the intended thing clearly. “The blue tray” can be enough; extra details should serve the reader.
3. Can a text be correctly spelt but still need editing?
Yes. The events might be out of order, a pronoun might be unclear or a reason might not support the request.
faq: What makes a persuasive reason useful?
It connects to the request and matters to the reader. Different views can be supported; you do not have to share the model’s preference.
Do I need to make every version digitally?
No. Paper is a useful route. To practise the digital elaboration, use an adult-supported tool to actually create, rearrange and revise a text.
modelCaption: Choose the job, draft the message, then improve it

title: Prepare, rehearse and share a short talk
intro: I can organise a short presentation, practise with a listener and adjust my delivery to help my audience.
exampleTitle: A useful opening tells listeners what is coming
example: Original presentation for classmates: “Today I will explain how our reading box works. First, choose one book from the box. Next, return it with its cover facing the front. This helps the next reader find a book. Thank you for listening.” The opening names the topic; first and next organise the directions; the ending explains their purpose. An adult models it aloud, pausing between the steps. Reading these delivery notes alone does not demonstrate speaking.
steps: 1. Plan for a familiar audience and purpose

Choose what the listeners need to know. Put an opening, related points and an ending in a useful order. Use accurate topic words and language that suits the occasion. More formal school language can be clear and polite without using difficult words.

Casual rehearsal note: “Here’s our book box.” A clear opening for a visiting class is “Welcome. I will explain how to choose and return a book.” Both can suit their contexts. The second states the purpose for visitors.

Use these model facts for a short class report: the reading box is beside the mat; it holds books for quiet reading; return each book with its cover facing the front. Give an opening, two useful points and an ending.

For example: “Today I will describe our reading box. It is beside the mat and holds books for quiet reading. Please return each book with its cover facing the front. That helps our class use the box.” Other clear sequences are valid. Keep the supplied facts and explain the purpose.
2. Rehearse with a useful cue and a listener
A cue reminds you what comes next. It can be a few words, a drawing or a simple diagram. Rehearse the actual talk, ask what the listener understood and change one feature before trying again.

Cue words for the reading-box demonstration: “Choose → Read → Return”. Draw three boxes with those labels and point to each as you explain it. If a listener says “I missed how to return the book”, pause before that step and explain the cover direction again.
Make the three-box cue on paper. Rehearse your talk, ask “What should you do when you finish reading?” and use the listener’s answer to choose one improvement.

The listener should explain the return step. If it is unclear, change the words, cue or pause, then rehearse again. Note the actual feedback and the change made. A good-looking cue is support for the talk; it does not by itself show that the talk was delivered.
3. Deliver with purposeful tone, volume and pace

Tone is the attitude you convey; volume helps the audience hear; pace and pauses give time to follow. Adjust these to the setting and listener. There is no single pitch pattern or loudness that fits every speaker and occasion.

An adult models “Please put the books here” as a friendly invitation, then as a calm reminder to handle the books carefully. Discuss how each delivery fits its situation. For the reading-box talk, use an audible, comfortable volume and pause between choose and return.
Deliver the short reading-box presentation to a familiar listener. Try the welcome and care reminder too. Ask what the listener understood and whether the pace and volume helped.

Look for an organised message, useful topic words and delivery that suits the stated purpose. Accept different natural voices and appropriate access modes. If a listener misses a step, slow or pause there, clarify it and try again. Judge the actual performance, not a printed choice about delivery.
mistakes: “Louder is always clearer.”
Use comfortable volume for this listener and room. Clear wording, sensible pace and useful pauses also help.
“A cue must contain every word.”
Short words or a meaningful drawing can help you keep the order. A full script is also useful support while learning.
“Rehearsing means saying it unchanged again.”
Listen to specific feedback, improve one useful feature and try the changed version.
activityTitle: Plan it, practise it, share it
activity: Use the complete book-return or paper-fold presentation card in More examples. Prepare an opening, ordered points, a useful cue and an ending. Rehearse with an adult or partner, ask a specific question about what they understood, improve one feature and deliver the changed version.
adjust: Starter: an adult models a different short talk and helps you use two cues. Core: organise and deliver your own short talk with a cue and one feedback-based improvement. Stretch: adapt the same message for a familiar visiting class, explaining changes to your opening, tone or pace.
safety: Use spoken language, AAC or agreed communication support. Record what was modelled or prompted. Do not grade eye contact, accent, standing still or a fixed speaking speed. Written planning can support the learning; actual delivery needs observation in the chosen mode.
tricky: 1. Can the same words sound welcoming or like a reminder?
Yes. Context and delivery can change the attitude listeners hear. Model both, ask the listener what they understood and avoid treating one pitch pattern as a universal rule.
2. Does reading every cue prove the audience understood?
No. Ask the listener to explain the main point or steps. Use their response to check and improve clarity.
3. Must I keep speaking if the listener is confused?
Pause, find the unclear part and explain or show it differently. That is a useful delivery adjustment.
faq: How long must the talk be?
Keep it short enough to organise and deliver comfortably. The goal is a clear purposeful presentation, not a universal time or speed target.
Can a visual help?
Yes, if you actually refer to it and it explains or cues something useful. A decorative picture alone does not organise the message.
modelCaption: A cue supports the talk; a listener helps you improve it

title: Write clear words with growing ease
intro: I can write recognisable unjoined letters, leave useful word spaces and check my handwriting while staying comfortable.
exampleTitle: Word spaces make a message easier to read
example: The typed examples below show spacing only: “Miahasabluebag.” and “Mia has a blue bag.” The second separates the five words. To practise handwriting, an adult first writes that sentence in the unjoined style taught at school. Watch the actual movements, then copy beside the model on suitable paper. A computer font is a target to read, not proof of handwriting or a stroke-order guide.
steps: 1. Watch the taught movement, then write

Use a nearby school-approved unjoined letter model. Watch where each letter starts and how it moves, then write it yourself. Upper-case and lower-case forms can look different. Keep the letters unjoined and recognisable.

An adult writes “Mia” and “mia” using the learner’s taught forms. Compare the capital M with lower-case m, then watch each movement. The capital version can name a person. Copy both for a case comparison; an adult observes the actual writing.
With an adult’s handwritten model beside you, write “Sam” and “bag” without tracing. What should the adult check?

The intended letters should be recognisable, in the supplied order and case, using unjoined taught forms. The adult also observes starting points and movement where these are being taught. Accept the school’s consistent forms rather than demanding an exact computer-font match.
2. Place letters and leave word spaces

Use the paper guides that help you. Letter bodies relate to a baseline; some letters reach up and parts of others reach below it. Keep letters close enough to form words, with clearer gaps between words.

An adult writes “a big bag” in the taught style on suitable lines. The a has a short body, b reaches up, and parts of g reach below the baseline. Compare this with the adult’s capital B. The whole letter does not have to stay above the line.
Copy the adult’s model “Sam has a red mug.” Leave clear word gaps and compare a short letter, a tall letter and a letter with a part below the baseline.

Look for recognisable unjoined words, sensible relative sizes and clear spaces. For example, a has a short body, d reaches up and g has a part below the baseline. Use the local model to check the actual forms; do not force every letter into the same height.
3. Build comfortable fluency and check your work

Practise a small useful target accurately, then use it in a word or sentence. A functional grasp lets you control the tool comfortably. Support your arm and paper in a position that works for you; different hands and suitable adapted tools may need different arrangements.

After writing “Mia has a blue bag.”, circle one clear word and choose one feature to improve, such as the gap after has. Write it again in another short session under similar conditions. Compare readable letter forms, gaps and ease of movement.
Write the adult-modelled sentence “We put a bag here.” Then choose one strength and one improvement. What evidence would show growing ease over time?

Use the actual handwritten sample to identify a clear feature and a specific next step. Growing ease needs comparable attempts over time, with less hesitation or effort while the words remain readable. One quick or copied page alone does not prove growth. There is no single speed target for everyone.
mistakes: “A capital is just a bigger lower-case letter.”
Some shapes differ. Watch and use the taught upper-case and lower-case forms.
“Every part of every letter stays above the line.”
Parts of letters such as g, p or y can go below the baseline. Check the school model.
“Only one pencil grasp is allowed.”
The aim is comfortable control. Follow individual school or specialist guidance and observe the learner writing.
activity: Prepare a comfortable pencil or agreed adapted tool, suitable paper and an adult’s school-style handwritten model. Write “Mia has a blue bag.” and “We put a bag here.” without tracing. Circle one clear word, choose one useful target and practise it briefly. Keep a dated sample and compare another short attempt later.
adjust: Starter: watch and copy one familiar word beside the model. Core: write a short mixed-case sentence with clear unjoined forms and spaces. Stretch: write a short label or message, then revise one feature while keeping the writing comfortable and readable.
safety: Use the learner’s preferred writing hand and appropriate support. A comfortable functional grasp matters more than one prescribed finger arrangement. Stop and ask an adult for help if writing hurts or causes strain. Typing, selecting a picture or naming a grip does not demonstrate handwritten formation.
tricky: 1. Can a neat typed answer prove my handwriting?
No. It can show the intended words. The handwritten result and, for movement or grasp, observation of writing provide the relevant evidence.
2. Should I make all letters exactly the same height?
No. Relative body height, tall parts and parts below the baseline vary. Follow the taught unjoined style and suitable line guides.
3. Is the fastest copy always the best?
No. Growing fluency means increasing ease while maintaining readable words, rather than rushing or comparing everyone with one speed.
faq: Must I change my writing hand?
No. Use the hand that works for you, with paper position and support that suit your needs.
What if my school’s a or g looks different from the screen?
Use the consistent form taught at school. The typed examples here show word targets or spacing, not a compulsory handwriting script.
modelCaption: Typed spacing comparison; practise the real handwriting with a nearby adult-written model

title: Change sounds to make new words
intro: I can hear the sounds in a word, change the sound asked for, then read and write the new word.
exampleTitle: Keep the other sounds in order
example: An adult says clamp. Hear five sounds: /k/, /l/, the short vowel in cat, /m/, /p/. Remove only /l/. Four sounds remain and blend to camp. After saying the answer, look at clamp and camp: the spelling records the change. For a new oral task, turn the screen away so the learner hears the word before seeing print.
steps: 1. Blend and segment spoken words
Blend means join sounds to say a word. Segment means separate the spoken word into its sounds. Move one counter for each phoneme, even when two letters later spell that sound.

An adult models fresh as /f/, /r/, the vowel in bed, /sh/: four sounds. In spoon, /s/ and /p/ stay separate; oo later spells one vowel sound. Cloudy has two syllables when spoken naturally, but five phonemes: /k/, /l/, the vowel in cloud, /d/, the final vowel in happy. Syllables and phonemes count different things.
Adult: say stamp without showing its spelling. Learner: segment it with counters, then blend the sounds back together. How many counters do you need?

Five: /s/, /t/, the vowel in cat, /m/, /p/. Blending all five in order gives stamp. If a sound is missing, the adult models it and the learner tries again; record that support. Show the printed word only after the oral turn.
2. Remove exactly the sound named
Say the word, find the named sound, remove its counter and blend what remains. A sound may occur inside a consonant cluster. Keep the other sounds in their original order.
Say slip without its first /s/: lip remains. Say best without /s/: bet remains, because the final /t/ stays. Say tent without its final /t/: ten remains. These examples remove one phoneme each.
Adult: say bend. Ask the learner to say it without /n/, without showing the printed word. What word remains?

Bed remains: /b/, the vowel in bed, /d/. The middle /n/ was removed; the final /d/ was kept. Once the learner has said bed, ask them to write it and read their spelling back. Check oral manipulation and spelling separately.
3. Swap a sound, then link it to print
Substitute means swap the specified phoneme for another. Say and compare the old and new words. Then use known sound spellings to write the new word and reread it.

Change /r/ in fresh to /l/: flesh. Change the last /p/ in clap to /m/: clam. To change stack to stick, swap the vowel in cat for the vowel in sit; keep /s/, /t/, /k/ in order. An adult models actual sounds rather than adding a spoken uh after each consonant.
Adult: say slam and ask for its vowel to change to the vowel in sit. After the oral answer, ask the learner to write the new word and read it back.

Slim. Only the vowel changed. The spelling is s-l-i-m. If the oral answer is correct but the spelling is not, keep the successful sound change and teach the missing sound–letter match. Use the learner’s consistent local pronunciation.
mistakes: Counting letters instead of sounds
In fresh, sh spells one sound. In its fr cluster, /f/ and /r/ are two sounds. Listen before counting.
Removing a whole cluster when one sound was named
In clamp, removing /l/ leaves camp. Removing both /k/ and /l/ would be a different instruction.
Reading a displayed answer as proof of hearing the change
Use a fresh adult-spoken turn with print covered, then a separate reading and writing turn.
activityTitle: Hear it, change it, write it
activity: Use counters, paper and a pencil. The adult first models one sound change from the lesson. Turn the screen away for the fresh oral tasks in More examples. The learner says each result before seeing print, then writes and rereads it. Finish by asking which sound changed. Keep a note of independent responses and any model or prompt needed.
adjust: Starter: use counters with a modelled three-sound word. Core: remove or swap one phoneme in a cluster word. Stretch: perform two named changes in turn, explaining each, then write and reread the final word.
safety: An adult must supply clear spoken sounds and accept consistent local pronunciation. Written notation and automatic text-to-speech are not substitutes for a checked sound model. Use an agreed accessible response mode and record the support.
tricky: Does sh in ship need two sound counters because it has two letters?
No. It spells one phoneme. Ship has three sounds: /sh/, the vowel in sit, /p/.
Say nest without /s/. What must stay at the end?
Net; /t/ stays at the end. Only /s/ is removed.
An adult says clap. Change only its last sound to /m/. Is the answer clam or camp?
Clam. Camp would also change the order and middle consonant sounds.
faq: Can a task remove more than one sound?
Yes, if it explicitly asks for that sequence. The beginning scr in scratch represents several phonemes; it must not be called one sound. First learn one specified change clearly.
How do I know the learner can do it independently?
Use a fresh spoken word without a displayed answer or advance reading model. Observe the actual response, then check writing and rereading separately.
modelCaption: Spoken model: remove only the second sound from clamp.

title: Read and spell words using sound patterns
intro: I can use sound–letter matches, silent letters and familiar word parts to read and spell words.
exampleTitle: A spelling pattern can cross several letters
example: In night, n spells /n/, igh spells the long i sound and t spells /t/. Blend the three phonemes. In rain, r and n each spell a consonant sound, while ai spells the long a sound. Read the whole printed word, then check that it makes sense. A picture is not a replacement for reading its letters.
steps: 1. Notice vowel spellings
A vowel digraph has two letters working together to spell a vowel sound. Some long vowel spellings use more letters. Learn a pattern in real words, then blend the complete word.

Read green, moon, rain, play and beach. They show ee, oo, ai, ay and ea. Night shows the less common igh spelling for long i; its final t still spells /t/. Patterns can have alternatives: oo differs in moon and book, and ea differs in beach and bread. An adult models unfamiliar pronunciations.
Read light. Which letters spell its long i sound, and which letter spells the last sound?
Igh spells the long i sound; t spells the final /t/. L spells the first sound. Blend all three phonemes to read light. Do not treat ight as one phoneme.
2. Keep cluster sounds; notice silent letters
In a consonant cluster you can hear each consonant phoneme. Some other spellings contain a letter that is not pronounced separately. Look carefully, blend the sounds and remember the written pattern.

In frog, /f/ and /r/ are separate sounds. In knee, k is not pronounced separately; kn spells /n/ and ee spells the vowel. In thumb, th spells one first sound and b is not pronounced separately at the end. We still include the silent letters when spelling.
Read crisp and knock. Which starts with two separate consonant sounds, and which has a silent initial k?

Crisp begins /k/, /r/: a consonant cluster. Knock begins /n/; the initial k is silent in this word. Read both words fully. When spelling knock, remember the kn pattern even though no separate /k/ is heard.
3. Blend longer words and familiar parts
Use known sound patterns through the whole word. A familiar compound can be split into two complete words, read and joined. Other longer words can be read in manageable syllables.

Raincoat combines rain and coat; both parts help us read and spell the whole word. Sunset combines sun and set. Rabbit has two spoken syllables, rab–bit; its two written b letters do not require two separate /b/ sounds. Join the parts smoothly and check the meaning.
Read lunchbox. Which two complete words help you, and how would you spell the word meaning a box for lunch?
Lunch and box combine to make lunchbox, written as one word here. Read both parts, join them and reread the whole word. Spelling it requires the letters in both parts, including the ch in lunch.
mistakes: Saying one sound for an entire cluster
In frog, keep both /f/ and /r/. In sh, the two letters work together for one phoneme.
Leaving out a silent letter when writing
Read knee with no separate /k/, but keep k in its conventional spelling.
Expecting a vowel spelling to have only one sound
Compare the actual words: oo in moon differs from oo in book. Blend a plausible reading and check the meaning.
activityTitle: Read, sort and spell a fresh word
activity: Read the supplied word cards in More examples. Sort by a feature you can explain; a word may belong in more than one group. Then turn the cards away. The adult dictates a different word from the closed adult card. The learner says its sounds, writes it, checks the spelling and rereads the written word. Copying an open card is practice; use the covered turn to check independent spelling.
adjust: Starter: read a few taught vowel-pattern words with sound boxes. Core: combine vowels, clusters and silent-letter words. Stretch: explain the parts of a two-syllable or compound word, then independently spell a fresh example.
safety: Use words containing patterns already taught to the learner. Accept consistent local spoken forms. An adult checks actual reading and dictated spelling; choosing a label alone does not demonstrate either performance.
tricky: In night, do gh add two more spoken sounds?
No. Igh spells the long i vowel here. The word has three phonemes: /n/, long i, /t/.
Should the spelling of thumb leave out b because we cannot hear a separate /b/?
No. The conventional spelling still includes b. Notice and remember the mb pattern at the end.
Does seeing rain inside raincoat mean you may skip the other letters?
No. Read rain and coat, then join and check the complete word.
faq: Can a word fit two sorting groups?
Yes. Raincoat has a vowel digraph and is a compound. Explain the feature you used instead of forcing one label.
Are all two-syllable words compounds?
No. Sunset contains two complete words, sun and set. Rabbit has two syllables but does not split into two complete words with those meanings.
modelCaption: Three phonemes in night: n, the long i vowel, and t.

title: Use patterns and word parts for tricky spellings
intro: I can use sounds, known spelling patterns and meaningful word parts to read and write less predictable words.
exampleTitle: Learn the unexpected part, keep the useful clues
example: Say said. S and d match its first and last sounds. The middle vowel sounds like the vowel in bed, but is written ai. Notice that exact part, write said from memory with the model covered, then check and reread it. Do not replace the whole word with a guess when some parts already give useful clues.
steps: 1. Find known sounds and an unusual part
Say the word, map the sounds you know and mark the unexpected spelling. Read it in a short sentence. Cover the model, write the word and compare the exact letters.

In said, ai spells the vowel in bed. In friend, ie also spells that short vowel. These words keep useful consonant sound clues. Come and have end in e, yet they do not follow a rule that every final e makes the preceding vowel long. Learn the particular word and pattern.
Read: “My friend said hello.” Which vowel spelling needs remembering in friend, and which in said?

Friend uses ie for the vowel in bed; said uses ai for that vowel. The written patterns differ even though the vowels sound alike in these words. Read the sentence, then cover it before writing either word from an adult’s dictation.
2. Use meaningful parts to preserve spelling
A morpheme is a meaningful word part. A known base or ending can guide spelling even when its pronunciation varies. Check the join rather than writing only what the ending sounds like.

Jump + ed makes jumped: the ending sounds like /t/. Play + ed makes played: the ending sounds like /d/. Want + ed makes wanted: the ending adds a syllable. All three use ed to mark past time here. Knowing friend also helps with friendly: keep the letters friend and add ly.
Write the past form of help in: “Yesterday I ___ Mum.” Why does its ending use ed?
Helped. It means the helping happened in the past. The ending sounds like /t/, but its spelling is ed: help + ed. The base help stays visible. Reread the complete sentence to check meaning.
3. Check a plausible reading with context
Sometimes the same printed word has more than one pronunciation. Read all its letters, try a plausible pronunciation and use the sentence meaning to choose. Then reread smoothly.

“The wind blew the leaves.” Wind has the vowel in sit. “Please wind the toy.” Wind rhymes with find because it means turn or coil here. Both readings match the printed word; the rest of each sentence tells us which meaning is needed.
Read these sentences aloud: “I will read the note tomorrow.” “Yesterday I read the note.” How does read change?

In the first sentence read rhymes with seed; in the second it rhymes with bed. Will and tomorrow point to future reading; yesterday points to past reading. The spelling stays read. The adult listens to the actual reading before revealing this response.
mistakes: Trying to sound out every word using one rigid rule
Keep the useful sound clues and learn the particular unexpected pattern, as with ai in said.
Spelling every past ending as it sounds
Jumped, played and wanted all keep ed here, although the endings sound different.
Guessing a different printed word from the sentence
Context helps choose between plausible readings of the letters you can see. It does not permit changing those letters.
activityTitle: Map it, cover it, spell it
activity: Use the complete word and sentence cards in More examples. Read each, point to a useful sound match or meaningful part and explain the part to remember. Then hide the model. The adult dictates a fresh target and the learner writes and rereads it. Finish by reading the paired sentences aloud. Note actual reading and spelling separately from copied or prompted work.
adjust: Starter: practise one common word with its unexpected part marked. Core: independently read and spell a related word using a known base or ed ending. Stretch: read the same-spelling sentence pair and explain how context selects the pronunciation.
safety: An adult supplies the spoken dictation target with the model covered and listens to the learner. Accept consistent local pronunciation. Reading or writing supports should be recorded so supported success is clear.
tricky: Must ai always have the vowel heard in rain?
No. In said it spells the vowel in bed. A useful common pattern is not a rule for every word.
Should helped end in the single letter t because that is the last sound?
No. Its past ending is spelled ed: help + ed. The base and ending guide the written form.
May you read wind as breeze because the sentence is about weather?
No. Breeze is a different printed word. Use the weather meaning to choose the suitable pronunciation of wind while keeping its letters.
faq: Does high-frequency mean a word is impossible to sound out?
No. It means the word occurs often. Some are regular; others have an unexpected part. Analyse each rather than memorising every word as an unexplained shape.
Are one, once, only and lone pronounced alike because their letters overlap?
No. An adult models each: one and once begin with a /w/ sound; only and lone have the long o vowel. Compare the complete spellings and meanings. This is not a rule for simply adding ly to one.
modelCaption: Said: useful first and last sound clues, with the unexpected middle spelling ai.
modelCards: s · first sound as in sun
d · last sound as in dog

title: Build meaningful word families
intro: I can add a prefix or suffix to a known base, explain the new meaning and use the family to spell a word.
exampleTitle: Keep the base and explain what changes
example: Cover means put something over. Un + cover makes uncover, meaning remove a covering or reveal something. Cover + ing makes covering, as in “I am covering the box.” The base cover connects the family through meaning and helps us keep its spelling. Simply sharing a rhyme is not enough.
steps: 1. Add a prefix before the base
A prefix is a meaningful part added at the start of a base. Read the new word and check what the prefix changes. Use a conventional word that makes sense.

Re + play makes replay: play again. Un + kind makes unkind: not kind. In unzip, un means reverse the zipping action. Notice the meaning in its sentence rather than assuming un has exactly the same effect in every word.
Use re and tell to build a word meaning tell again. Write it in “Please ___ the story.”
Retell: re + tell. “Please retell the story.” The prefix re comes before tell and adds the idea again. Keep all the letters in the base tell, then reread the sentence.
2. Add a suffix after the base
A suffix is a meaningful ending added after a base. It can change meaning or the way a word is used. Keep track of both the new spelling and what the whole word means.

Help + er makes helper, someone who helps. Help + ful makes helpful, giving help. Friend + ly makes friendly, acting like a friend; friend + ship makes friendship, the relationship between friends. In each pair the familiar base helps with spelling.
Starting with help, write a word for someone who helps. Then write a different family word for giving help.

Helper and helpful. Both keep help. Er means someone who does the action in helper; ful contributes the helpful quality in helpful. Use each in a sensible sentence, such as “The helper carried the bag” and “That was a helpful idea.”
3. Check the family, then spell and use a new word
A meaningful family shares a base and connected meanings. Find the base, decide which added part matches your message, write the conventional word and reread it in a sentence.

Play, replay and player share the meaning of play. Day rhymes with play, but it is not built from the base play. Cover, covering and uncover share the base cover. Not every base accepts every ending, so check that your new word is used with that meaning.
You know friend. Write the word meaning the relationship between friends in “Their ___ grew as they played together.” Explain the parts.

Friendship: friend + ship. Keep friend, including its ie spelling, and add ship. “Their friendship grew as they played together.” The ending here names a relationship; it is not the separate boat meaning of ship.
mistakes: Grouping words only because they rhyme
Play and day rhyme, but day is not built from play. Look for a shared meaningful base.
Treating matching first letters as a prefix
Un in unkind changes kind to not kind. Uncle is not made from un plus a base cle with that meaning.
Adding any ending without checking meaning
Build a conventional word and try it in a sentence. Different suffixes can produce different valid family words.
activityTitle: Make a word family and use it
activity: Use the supplied base and affix cards in More examples. Build several conventional words, put prefixes before and suffixes after the base, then explain each meaning in a sentence. Hide the completed models for the fresh spelling turn. The adult gives a meaning and the learner builds, writes and rereads a suitable family word.
adjust: Starter: choose between a prefix and suffix card for one modelled base. Core: build and explain two different words in a family. Stretch: combine un + help + ful to make unhelpful, explain how each part contributes and use it in a meaningful sentence.
safety: Accept different conventional words when they satisfy an open prompt and the learner explains their meaning. Check actual spelling and sentence use. A correct card choice alone does not demonstrate independent writing.
tricky: Are play and day in the same morphemic family because they rhyme?
No. Day does not contain the base play or its meaning. Player and replay do.
In replay, where is the prefix and what does it add?
Re is before play. It adds again, so replay means play again.
Can friendly help you spell friendship?
Yes. Both use the base friend, keeping its ie spelling. Change the ending to match the new meaning: ly for friendly and ship for friendship.
faq: Does adding a suffix always leave the base spelling untouched?
No. These starter examples keep the base visible. Some other words change at the join; learn those patterns with an adult instead of assuming every word joins in the same way.
Is a word family the same as a list of synonyms?
No. Kind and nice can have related meanings without sharing a base. Kind, unkind and kindness form a meaningful family built around kind.
modelCaption: The cover family keeps a meaningful base while prefixes and suffixes change the message.
